Multiple thunderstorms move over Lorain County between the 25th and 26th of May. The storms on the 25th saturated the ground, allowing for rapid runoff from storms on the 26th. A storm moved over Lorain County late on the 26th with rainfall rates over an inch per hour. Numerous roads were flooded and several were closed. In the hardest hit city of Lorain there was waist deep flooding in Gulf Street and Ohio Street near the elementary school.

Multiple thunderstorms move over Lorain County between the 25th and 26th of May. The storms on the 25th saturated the ground, allowing for rapid runoff from storms on the 26th. A storm moved over Lorain County late on the 26th with rainfall rates over an inch per hour. Numerous roads were flooded and several were closed. In Elyria, water several feet deep was reported over Poplar and Olive Streets.

Multiple thunderstorms move over central Ohio. A strong storm with rainfall rates over an inch per hour hit late on the 25th. Numerous roads were flooded and several were closed. In Crestline some families had to be evacuated to to rising flood waters from a local creek.

Multiple thunderstorms move over central Ohio on the evening of the 25th. A storm moved over Ashland County late on the 25th with rainfall rates over an inch per hour. Numerous roads were flooded and several were closed. Water rescuse had to be conducted along RT 250 and Rt 89 as flood waters from Scotts Run inundated the road.

Thunderstorms with efficient rainfall rates moved over Cuyahoga County. Doppler Radar estimated over two inches of rainfall withing 75 minutes fell over portions of the county. Olmsted Falls experienced widespread flooding as streams downtown overflowed their banks. Water several feet deep was reported over Cook Road in the northern portion of town.

Strong thunderstorms with hail and heavy rain moved over Lorain County. The town of Pittsfield had high water on several roads most notably Quarry Road and Russia Road where depths were near waist deep in spots. Doppler Radar estimated over 2.5 in this area over 2 hours.

Strong thunderstorms with rain, wind, and hail moved over portions of Lorain County. Rainfall rates approaching two inches per hour were reported with this storm. Flooding occurred in Oberlin with several roads impassable with water up to the hoods on cars.

Heavy rain fell over portions of Trumbull County on the 25th and 26th of May. Doppler Radar estimates around two to three inches of rain fell over a 24hr span, with the majority of the rain falling in two seperate showers lasting less than an hour a piece. The runoff from the rainfall overwhelmed the Niles Water Department which had to close due to too much water.

Severe thunderstorms moved through Hancock County bringing strong winds and hail. The heavy rainfall also produced nuisance flooding in typical urban locations with water around two feet deep over Bigelow Avenue.

Strong thunderstorms with efficient rainfall moved over portions of Wood County on the 26th. Doppler Radar estimated as much as 2-3 inches of rain fell across portions of the county. Minor flooding resulted with several road closures for a few hours that evening. Some roads that were flooded include ST RT 65 and Brillhart Road.

Torrential thunderstorms moved over western Medina County on the 25th with rainfall rates around 1.5 inches per hour. Runoff from this excessive rainfall caused portions of Interstate 71 northbound to flood just north of State Route 83. It was impassable to cars and was closed for a short while.

Torrential rainfall with rates over an inch per hour produced widespread flooding across Stark County. The Ohio and Erie Canal towpath in Navarre was flooded and closed for a short while. Several roads were closed or experienced nuisance flooding from High St and Whipple Road NW in Canton, and Strausser St in Jackson Township.

Thunderstorms with wind, hail, and heavy rain passed through Lorain County during the afternoon hours. Heavy rainfall produced some minor flooding across the Oberlin area with some road closures. State Route 58 and U.S. Highway 20 south of Oberlin were flooded.

Thunderstorms with torrential rain moved over northern Ohio on the 25th. Rainfall rates around 1.5 per hour were observed. This heavy rainfall caused a mudslide in Garfield Heights closing portions of I-480 eastbound.

Thunderstorms with torrential rainfall with rates as high as 1.5 per hour moved over northern Ohio. Doppler radar estimated around two inches over Summit County. The rapid runoff resulted in flooding of several roads, including RT 224 and 277 in Akron.

Thunderstorms with torrential rainfall of over 1.5 per hour fell over northern Ohio. Doppler Radar estimated two to three inches of rainfall over the Akron area. Local rain gages reported 1.92 at Akron-Fulton Airport and 2.37 at the Akron COOP site. The result of this rainfall was several intersections and N Main Street flooded. Water depths were a foot or less.

Strong to severe thunderstorms with torrential rain moved over Northern Ohio on the 25th. Over Sandusky County as much as 2.13 inches of rain was recorded at the Fremont Water Treatment Plant during the evening hours. Runoff from these showers cause small streams and creeks to come out of banks during the early morning hours of the 26th. The Green Creek, a tributary to the Sandusky River, came out of banks and flooded County RT 181.

Showers and thunderstorms along a stationary front brought around 1.5 of rainfall to Portage County. Recent rain prevented the ground from absorbing much if any of this rain, resulting in almost complete runoff. Several streets were inundated with as much as a foot of water, and the Atwater Water Treatment Plant experienced flooding.

Saturated ground conditions from recent rains set the stage for flooding on the 24th as a cold front moved into Stark County. Showers developed along this boundary, with rainfall amounts recorded at 0.80 inches in NE Canton and 0.50 inches in NW Canton. Though not a significant amount of rainfall, it became almost entirely runoff. The result was flooding of several roads, mainly in the Canton and Massillon Areas. Some roads flooded include RT21 from Lake to Cherry St. in Massillon along with Fire Station #4. Most of the rainfall fell within 30 minutes, so the rate of the rainfall contributed to the level of flooding.

An area of low pressure and associated frontal boundaries resulted in several days of showers and thunderstorms with high rainfall rates. This rainfall cumulated over saturated ground cover to produce countywide flooding in Trumbull County. Several streams and creeks came out of banks, including the Eagle Creek in Braceville. In the Vienna and Howland areas there were several basements flooded.

Torrential rain from passing thunderstorms brought as much as 2.5 or rain to portions of Cuyahoga County. This intense rainfall over saturated grounds produced rapid runoff. The result was several roads flooded, including Smith Road in Middleburg Heights where several inches of flowing water was observed. Portions of Westlake, Parma, and Garfield Heights experienced flooding in non-typical places as well. West 130th St in Cleveland Ohio was impassable due to flash flooding when several feet of flowing water filled the road in 10 minutes.

Two seperate severe thunderstorms brought strong winds, hail, and torrential rain to Hancock County. The heaviest rainfall from the first storm fell over Findlay with as much as 1.75 in 75 minutes. The second storm followed shortly behind the first, but this time further south over Arlington. Doppler radar estimates as much as 2.5 fell in this area. The combined rainfall over the Eagle Creek watershed caused it to spill into downtown Arlington. In Arlington several roads were flooded, with two to three feet of water over South Main Street.

Torrential rain fell over portions of Marion County as severe thunderstorms moved through the region. Rainfall rates over an inch per hour produced rapid runoff with rapid filling of small streams and creeks. This resulted in the flooding of local roadways. Rocky Fork, Prairie Run, and Grave Creek came over their banks, some  by as much as 2.5 feet. The Marion County Engineers office says numerous county gravel roads were flooded and closed.

A series of strong to severe thunderstorms rolled through Seneca County, with strong winds, hail, and torrential rainfall. The rainfall resulted in flash flooding across the county. Sheriff's department reported water running across several roads with creeks coming out of their banks. Storm drains in the city of Tiffin were overwhelmed which caused water rises up to the hoods of cars downtown. A person had to be rescued as a result. A railroad underpass in Tiffin was flooded several feet deep.

Strong thunderstorms brought wind, hail, and torrential rain to Ashland County on the evening of the 14th. Doppler Radar estimated as much as 2 inches fell within two hours over northern portions of the county. The result was several roads flooded. Flood damage closed County Road 1302 between U.S. 42 and Township Road 753 in Montgomery Township.

Torrential rainfall with rates over an inch per hour fell over portions of western Crawford County. Though rainfall amounts were generally one to two inches, the rain rate combined with saturated ground conditions resulted in rapid runoff. The runoff resulted in flooded basements and roads. Cars stalled along highway 6 near Maples Road as water depths were over hoods.

Lorain County experienced their third straight day of flooding on the 14th. Storms brought around an inch of additional rainfall, but this in addition to already swollen streams and saturated ground cover was enough to trigger additional flooding. Several creeks came out of their banks and water was running across several roads. The speed that the water rose caught motorists by surprise as many cars stalled in high water.

Several days of heavy rain had led to saturated ground and swollen creeks and streams across Trumbull County. On the 14th line of thunderstorms brought an additional inch to an inch and a half of rainfall. This rainfall became almost enirely runoff, which rapidly flooded low lying and poor drainage areas. A car became stuck on the road on RT 40 near Leavittsburg, where water was also entering apartment buildings. Several roads had to be closed.

Several days of heavy rain set the stage for additional flooding on the 14th. Heavy rain with rates over an inch per hour resulted in flash flooding over portions of Portage County. Several roads had to be closed near Streetsboro including RT 303.

Torrential rain fell over Trumbull County on the evening of the 14th, this after three preceding days of flooding. The saturated ground could not handle additional rainfall, so the one to two inches that fell on this evenig resulted in flash flooding. Several creeks mainly in northern portions of the county came out of their banks. Basements flooded in the Howland Township area. Several roads were impassable including OH 193.

Saturated ground cover could not hold any additional rain, however on the evening of the 14th torrential rainfall brought an additional inch to Geauga County. The rain fell within 75 minutes, resulting in rapid runoff. The result was flash flooding mainly over northern portions of the county where rainfall was the heaviest. Several state and local roads were flooded including RT 528 in Parkman.

Overwhelmed drainage systems and saturated ground cover from recent floods and heavy rain set the stage for additional flooding on the 14th. A storm brought an inch or less of rainfall to the Youngstown area, however the high rate of rainfall was sufficient to produce flooding. Several roads in Youngstown flooded with up to a foot of water as drains backed up.

Storms with torrential rainfall combined with saturated ground conditions resulted in flash flooding over Ashtabula County. Several small streams and creeks were already swollen due to recent rains and floods, so the additional inch to an inch and a half was more than sufficient to produce flooding. Several creeks came out of banks, with portions of ST RT 46 closed as several inches of flowing water from a small creek near the town of Rock Creek covered the road.

An EF1 tornado touched down in a cemetery on the southeast side of Monroeville.  This tornado then continued east on the ground for about eight miles before lifting near the intersection of Tiger Road and North Greenwich Milan Road on the southeast side of Norwalk.  The path was parallel and just south of U.S. Route 20 for several miles.  Around a dozen homes and businesses were damaged by this tornado.  A couple of the buildings lost large sections of roofing with some of damage caused by fallen trees.  The tornado also leveled a large barn as it crossed Halfway Road.   Several dozen trees were also downed along the damage path which was no more than 50 yards in width.

An EF0 tornado touched down in Fairlawn and traveled northeast for over four miles before lifting for good near Cuyahoga Falls.  The damage survey suggested that the tornado may not have been in contact with the ground for much of the path length which was no more than 50 yards in width.  Only intermittent damage was observed and it is likely that some of this was caused by straight line winds.  Most of the damage was from fallen trees but some buildings were also damaged.  A church in Fairlawn lost it's roof and several buildings sustained roof damage in downtown Cuyahoga Falls.  Dozens of trees were either uprooted or snapped by the tornado.   Several witnesses reported seeing a tornado in contact with the ground.

Ten homes and buildings along the damage path sustained damage, mainly from lost roofing or siding.  Many trees were also downed.  Straight line winds may have contributed to the damage path which was no more than 100 yards in width.

A house near the high school lost a large section of roof.  Another 8 to 10 homes were damaged in a neighborhood just to the west of South Myers Road and to the south of U.S. 20.  Most of this damage was caused by fallen trees and limbs.  Many trees were damaged along the damage path which was over a mile in length.

Around ten homes and buildings were damaged along the damage path which was no more than 100 yards in width.  Most of the damage was from lost roofing or siding.  Many trees were also downed along the damage path.

Lake enhanced rainfall over Erie County produced torrential rainfall with rates around two inches per hour. As much as 3 to 5 inches of storm total rain fell over the city of Sandusky. Several underpasses filled with water and many roads were closed due to high water.

An official NWS observer reported 2.3 of rain in Oak Harbor in a matter of a few hours. This rainfall over already saturated ground resulted in widespread minor flooding. Several roads in downtown Oak Harbor were flooded with high water up to a foot deep.

Two to three inches of rain fell over central Trumbull County, all within three hours. Apartment complex on Lake View Road flooded with a foot of water. Several roads were flooded and closed as a result of the rapid runoff.

Lake enhanced storms moved off Lake Erie dropping 2 to 3 inches within 90 minutes over Cuyahoga County. Radar estimated as much as 4 inches over a stretch from southern Westlake into Olmsted Falls and east into Berea. As a result drainage systems were overwhelmed and roads rapidly filled with over 3 feet of water. A water rescue was conducted in North Olmsted near the mall.

Rainfall amounts of 2 to 3.5 inches fell over Cleveland during a span of 60-90 minutes. Citywide flooding resulted as storm water systems were overwhelmed. Many roads including I 480 were flooded and closed for a brief period.

Torrential rainfall with rates around two inches per hour brought around 4 to 6 inches of rain to Summit County. The heaviest rain fell from Akron and to the north and western part of the county. The maximum daily total precipitation that was reported by an official NWS cooperative weather observer was 4.84 inches at the Akron-Canton Airport (CAK). CAK Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded the rain between 2:00 AM and 4:00 AM of around 4 inches, with additional rainfall thereafter.  This rainfall event frequency falls around a 500 year recurrence interval, or 0.2% chance of occurring in a single year.  The town of Copley also experienced significant flooding along the Pigeon Creek where the heaviest rain fell. An apartment complex was inundated and rescues were made. Hundreds of homes and businesses experienced basement flooding with a few first floors inundated as well. In the town of Green residents testified to a historic flood in Spade Road area.

The Nimishillen Creek, a tributary for the Tuscarawas River, reached major flood stage at the gage site in North Industry.  For the Nimishillen Creek, the majority of the rainfall fell over the western branch.  The west branch sub-watershed begins in Lake Township in northern Stark and near the Akron-Canton Regional Airport in the City of Green in Summit County.  Almost five inches of rain fell over the headwaters of the west branch that night, all of which drains into North Canton. A major tributary to the west branch is Zimber Ditch which begins around the Akron-Canton Airport and also flows directly south paralleling I-77 into Jackson Township.  Zimber Ditch has experienced more frequent flood problems over the last decade due to continued urban and suburban growth in the basin. Flooding along the Zimber Creek this event was responsible for a significant amount of the flood damage resulting in North Canton and downstream communities. The NWS forecast point for the Nimishillen Creek is located south of Canton in North Industry. By the time this site crested, the flooding was beginning to recede in Canton. By 9:00 AM the reported stage was of 11.14 FT and a flow over 6000 cfs, or major flood category.  This was the fifth highest flow for this gage site since records began in 1921.  Overal several hundreds of homes and businesses were flooded necessitating evacuations and moving residents into shelters which were opened earlier in response to the excessive heat the day before.  A number of water rescues were conducted, but no reports of injuries or fatalities.

Heavy rain fell over southern Cuyahoga County bringing 2 to 3 inches of rain over a 90 minute timeframe. In the Parma area the Big Creek overflowed its banks and flooded nearby businesses on Brookpark Road. Parma and Brooklyn Roads were also significantly flooded with two to three feet of water.

The maximum daily total precipitation that was reported by an official NWS cooperative weather observer was 4.84 inches at the Akron-Canton Airport (CAK). CAK Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded the rain between 2:00 AM and 4:00 AM of around 4 inches, with additional rainfall thereafter.  This rainfall event frequency falls around a 500 year recurrence interval, or 0.2% chance of occurring in a single year.  The heavy rain flooded the airport, shorting out the power supply. The automated rain gage failed at this point, but a backup rain gage observation supports the storm total. The basement of the airport flooded, along with the parking lots resulting in floating cars and significant damage to the vehicles. Flights were cancelled for half a day.

An official NWS observer measured 6.58 inches over Port Clinton on the 14th. Emergency Management estimates at least half the town experienced some form of flooding as storm sewer systems were overwhelmed. The H.B. Magruder Hospital was inundated with ankle deep flood waters. Many homes and businesses in Port Clinton observed water in their basements, garages, or into their first floors. Many residents report this to be the worse flooding since the July 4-5th storm of 1969. EMA estimated a lot of property was affected with minor flooding, very few major, and no destroyed.

Two to three inches of rain fell over Northern Lake County in 90-120 minutes resulting in flooding in Painesville. This rain fell over already saturated ground from the previous days one to two inches of rainfall, resulting in rapid runoff. The flooding was a result of sewer systems being overwhelmed and backing up into area roads. Several roads had one to two feet of water which lasted for several hours.

An area of strong low pressure passed well to the north of Lake Erie on January 1st. A strong cold front trailing the low swept east across Northeast Ohio late on the 1st. Cold west to northwest winds blowing across Lake Erie caused lake effect snow showers to develop during the late evening hours of the 1st. Bands of lake effect snow then continued into the afternoon hours of January 3rd before dissipating. The snow was locally heavy with visibilities at times less than a quarter mile. A peak total of 15.1 inches was reported at Pierpont. This was the first significant snow event of the season and resulted in difficult travel conditions.

Between 620 PM and 635 PM a torrential shower moved over the Beldon Village are in North Canton located just west of I-77. The shower lasted only 15 minutes, however during a 10 minute period rainfall rates jumped to 4.36 in/hr as estimated by NWS Doppler Radar. No gauges were located at the site of the flooding, but radar estimates put this rate around a 100 year rain for this part of Ohio. This extreme rate overwhelmed drainage systems with excessive runoff. The impact area was limited to a 1/4 to a 1/2 mile radius from the Beldon Village Mall. The parking lot of the mall with over 4 feet of water, manhole covers were blown off from the water pressure of the stormwater system, and several nearby roads flooded. A number of businesses were flooded including a grocery store and a fast food restaurant with as much as 2 feet of water. Several cars were flooded and one woman needed to be rescued. Storm total rainfall estimates were a little over an inch, however the extreme rainfall rates were the cause to the damage in this event.

An intense line of thunderstorms or Derecho moved across Hancock County during the afternoon of June 29th causing extensive damage.  A 84 mph wind gust was measured by an trained spotter in Findlay.  Over 75 percent of residents lost power during this event.  Power was not completely restored in Hancock County till July 6th.  Hundreds, if not thousands of trees were downed across the county along with many utility poles forcing the closure of dozens of roads and streets.  Damage to homes and buildings was also extensive.  In Findlay alone, 464 structures were damaged by the strong winds.  Of these, one building was destroyed with 15 other sustaining major damage and 43 with significant damage.  Much of this damage was from lost roofing or siding.  At least four semi trucks were blown over on Interstate 75 to the south of Findlay.  Clean up costs were extensive.  The clean up was hampered by an ongoing heat wave with afternoon temperatures as warm as 100 degrees.  Significant crop losses are also expected.  Damage from this storm was comparable to the remnants of Hurricane Ike in September 2008.

The Cuyahoga River at Independence experienced two crests during this event, both above major flood stage of 18.5 feet. The heaviest rain occurred during the evening of the 29th and again on the morning of the 31st. The rainfall rates were generally 0.1 to 0.2��� per hour, but during the heavier bands from Sandy rainfall rates jumped to almost 0.75��� per hour. The crest forecast called for a stage of 21 feet and the observed was 20.8 feet, 2.3 feet above major flood stage. The river was receding Tuesday but a band of heavy rain moved in Tuesday Night and Wednesday morning resulting in a second rise on the river. The second crest was 19.1 feet reached around noon Wednesday. Many roads in Valley View flooded. One vehicle was reported to have driven into the water and the driver had to be rescued. An estimated 20 homes had 3 to 4 feet of water, some as much as 6-7 feet, in their basements.

This event was unique for the Vermilion River, as well as most Lake Erie tributaries, as the water level along the lake rose about 2-3 feet above normal. Strong northerly gales combined with the higher water levels slowed discharge from the Vermilion River into the lake. The backup of water from the lake flooded portions along the Vermilion River near the mouth in a higher severity than was likely from the river alone. Several roads were closed and some minor property damage occurred. Along Riverside Drive the water came up about 2 to 3 feet above the street level flooding the garages and low lying property near the Vermilion River.

The Norwalk Reservoir located in Norwalk covers 8.6 square mile drainage area into the Norwalk Creek. The reservoir does not control outflow but does have a spillway on the west side when the reservoir is overtopped. Early Tuesday morning the reservoir filled and the water coming out of the spillway caused the Norwalk Creek to flood. One home on Elm Street flooded though several more were evacuated. Five businesses on Water Street were flooded with as much as 2 feet of water. Once driver was rescued after he drove his car into Water Street. Other local roads in Norwalk were flooded with no property damage.

The small community called Franklin Flats located along the Huron River in western Milan is frequently inundated during times of flood. During Superstorm Sandy the Huron River reached major flood stage at 21 feet during the night of the 30th. At this stage the river inundated Franklin Flats community with about 2 feet of water. Being flood prone, the homes are elevated and citizens in the area moved valuable property out of the flood zone prior to the inundation. The property damage was minimal as a result.

The Grand River at Painesville rose above flood stage early on the morning of the 30th and continued to rise to about 13.0 feet. The river flooded the high trafficked Vrooman Road shutting it down for two days. Some other low lying roads near the river flooded, but the only property inundation was near the mouth and was more lakeshore flooding than river flooding. Some basements were inundated from failed sump pumps.

The Black River at Elyria reached moderate flood stage during this event. The river rise was more gradual compared to climatology for this river due to the slow rainfall rates. The river came out of its banks and inundated Cascade Park, reaching some of the maintenance facilities. Damage was minimal.

Wind gusts in excess of 60 mph were reported for several hours by automated sensors at Cleveland Hopkins Airport and Burke Lakefront Airport.  A peak gust of 68 mph was measure at Hopkins Airport at 23:35 EDT.  Damage across Cuyahoga County was extensive with hundreds of trees and utility poles down.  Nearly 200,000 electric customers lost power in Cuyahoga County.  The western suburbs of Bay Village, Westlake and Rocky River were especially hard hit.  Dozens of streets had to be closed because of downed trees and power lines.  Many homes and vehicles sustained damage from downed trees and limbs.  Many homes also lost sections of roofing and siding.  Damage was reported at Burke Lakefront Airport and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame also sustained minor damage.  Also to note was a 2 to 3 foot storm surge along the south shore of Lake Erie accompanied by 15 to 20 foot waves. Water crashing over the break wall closed Interstate 90 on the east side of Cleveland for several hours. Area marinas sustained damage with reports of many personal watercraft submerged and additional boats drifting out into the lake. According to the Coast Guard, 118 vessels were either sunk or significantly damaged.

A four to six hour period of freezing rain occurred in Mahoning County.  Up to a third of an inch of ice accumulation was reported in the county. The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

A four to six hour period of freezing rain occurred in Portage County.  Between a quarter and a third of an inch of ice accumulation was reported in the county. The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

A four to six hour period of freezing rain occurred across inland Ashtabula County.  Up to a quarter inch of ice accumulation was reported across the southern third to half of the county. The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

A four to six hour period of freezing rain occurred with up to a quarter inch of ice accumulation reported. The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. An inch or two of snow accumulation was also reported on higher terrain. Strong southeast winds accompanied the precipitation with gusts as high as 35 mph reported. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

A four to six hour period of freezing rain occurred with up to a quarter inch of ice accumulation reported. The ice accumulated mainly on trees and grassy surfaces. An inch or two of snow accumulation was also reported on higher terrain. Strong southeast winds accompanied the precipitation with gusts as high as 35 mph reported. Some trees and limbs were toppled by the ice and there were also a few reports of power outages. A few accidents were reported.

A cold front swept east across the upper Ohio Valley on March 20th. Cold west to northwest winds developed behind the front causing lake effect snow showers to develop. The snow showers were intermittent and finally ended during the morning hours of the 22nd. The snow was heavy at times, especially during the afternoon and evening hours of the 21st when visibilities were less than a half mile at times. Winds gusted to more than 20 mph causing some blowing and drifting. Snowfall totals of 6 to 10 inches were reported across portions of inland Ashtabula County. A peak total of 12.3 inches was reported at Pierpont. Some accidents occurred.

Lake effect snow showers developed on the morning of March 20th and finally ended during the afternoon hours of the 22nd. The snow was heavy at times, especially during the afternoon and evening hours of the 21st when visibilities were less than a half mile at times. Winds gusted to more than 20 mph causing some blowing and drifting.  A peak total of 10.5 inches was reported near Meadville in Crawford County. A few accidents were reported.

Lake effect snow showers developed during the morning of March 20th and finally ended during the afternoon hours of the 22nd. The snow was heavy at times, especially during the afternoon and evening hours of the 21st when visibilities were less than a half mile at times. Winds gusted to more than 25 mph causing some blowing and drifting.  A few of the higher totals In Erie County included 18.0 inches south of North East, 17.3 inches at Franklin Center and 17.2 inches near Colt Station. A few accidents were reported.

Heavy rain fell over the higher terrain near Erie, PA. The runoff from the estimated 1 to 2.5 of rainfall in the basin was sufficient to flood several area roads. The off and on ramps for I-90 at the route 97 exit were shut down for several hours, starting at rush hour. Water depths were up to 6 feet in areas. One motorists had to be rescued after entering the flood waters. Water inundated two nearby gas stations underground storage tanks.

Rainfall measured between 4 and 5 inches feel over Greene, Summit, and McKean Townships in eastern Erie County on the 6th. This heavy rain, over saturated ground, produced widespread flooding. Elk Creek in McKean Township came out of it's banks and inundated a basement and garage at two different homes on Rick Road. Hamot Road was washed out on one side requiring road crews to make repairs. The water depth was estimated at a depth of three feet on some roads.
Law enforcement reported quarter size hail south of Mt. Cory.
Law enforcement reported quarter size hail near Milan.
A trained weather spotter reported half inch to one inch diameter hail fell for two minutes.
A trained weather spotter reported quarter size hail was covering the ground.
A National Weather Service employee reported quarter size hail.

The heavy rainfall caused about a 2 mile stretch of State Route 82 to flood with as much as  a foot of flowing water in Columbia station. At Snell Road and State Route 82 three motorists were pulled from a flooded intersection. A home on Parkwood Drive just south of Sprague Road and the Cuyahoga County line a home was inundated with a few feet of water on the first floor as the Baker Creek went from 6 feet wide to an estimated 500 feet wide onto the owners property. Several homes in Columbia Station, Olmsted Township, and Berea had basement flooding. In Berea, over 2 dozen homes were inundated when the sewer backed up from the overwhelmed storm drains.

Heavy rain pushed the Blanchard River in Findlay into major flood. The river crested just over 14 feet, more than a half a foot above major flood stage. The impacts were mainly isolated along the business district where the water inundated streets and some low lying basements. Homes along the Eagle Creek were threatened, but none were inundated.

In Tiffin, water reached between two and three feet behind Tiffin Mall on Westwood and Northwood drives. The residential area between Kroger and Miami Street was most affected as many homes had up to a foot of water in their basements. Roadways in Seneca County with high water included CR 26, east of SR 53, SR 18, west of 224 and SR 53 south of Fort Seneca.

Edinboro University of Pennsylvania campus was closed due to flash flooding between Earrly Hall to Hendricks Hall. Several roads were barricaded including Scotland Road, Heather Road, and Darrow Roads. Sand Bags were put in place to prevent inundation into buildings. Some minor water problems were reported in some of the buildings.
A home in Millcreek was flooded from water inundating the first floor and then into the basement.

The severe storms and heavy rains which hit Galion from Wednesday night and early Thursday morning caused more than $200,000 in damages in Galion. $100,000 in damages occurred to the Gospel Baptist Church. City firefighters evacuated seven residents on Sixth Avenue when knee-high flood waters rose around 11 p.m. at the single-story apartments. A residence on Grant Street flooded, leaving the home a total loss, according to Galion Police Department.

Upwards of 4.25 inches of rain fell across Ashtabula County, overwhelming drainage systems, flooding streets and roads, submerging basements and damaging property in communities south of Interstate 90. A Conneaut motorist was unhurt when her vehicle drove into high water on Broad Street. No weather-related injuries were reported, according to safety personnel. In the Ashtabula Harbor, water was knee-high at the intersection of West 9th Street and Thayer Avenue flooding the neighborhoods of Treelane, Saybula and Westshore drives. Several roadways and state highways were closed because of high water. Route 193 was shut down between routes 307 and 167 in the Dorset area, and Route 531 just east of Geneva-of-the-Lake.

Doppler Radar estimated over two inches of rain had fallen in southern and central Richland County between 430 pm and 600 pm. All Mansfield emergency agencies were called out as flash floods put parts of the city under water, delaying many of the weekend���s events, shutting down several area roads and even damaging a few. The city���s street department reported flooding closed down 12 intersections. All but the Park Avenue East underpass and Fourth Street and Bowman Avenue were opened by 10 p.m. Five vehicles stalled out trying to navigate rising waters at the underpass on Park Avenue East where within 20 minutes the water rose three feet. Fourth Street was blocked off at Bowman Avenue after flooding washed the blacktop down to the brick. The road has been under construction since Thursday. Mulberry Street also was closed at the railroad crossing after the heavy rain popped a piece of metal up off the tracks.
State route 89 was flooded in half a dozen spots and was closed. Several roads in Ashland were closed. Some local roads were washed out with the pavement removed.

Union City resides between two branches of the French Creek. The West Branch of the French Creek is located to the north and west of town and has a reservoir just before the confluence with the southern branch. The reservoir was constructed to retain excess runoff, mainly from spring snow melt. The reservoir water levels jumped over 30 feet as a result of the rain from this storm. Despite this, the southern branch of the French Creek, which runs through the southern part of town, came up quick and high. No gages are available on that tributary, but most of the flood damage was along this creek. The flooding that resulted was widespread through Union Township and the borough. Due to a road washout on Odell Street Ext. There were 7 rescues conducted with use of the fire truck ladder extended across the raging water. The flood damage was estimated over $100,000.

A supercell thunderstorm produced two tornadoes in Erie County.  The first tornado touched down about two miles northeast of Cranesville.  The tornado was on the ground for over a mile and a half and downed many trees.  A mobile home was also overturned and destroyed.  Five people inside the mobile home were injured.  A couple of farm buildings were also heavily damaged.   Peak winds were estimated to be around 90 mph making it an EF1 on the Enhanced Fujita scale.  The damage path was no more than 50 yards wide.

A second tornado touched down about two miles north of Edinboro.  This tornado then traveled east to Union city and finally lifted about three miles southeast of the town.  The tornado appears to have been on the ground only intermittently.  The damage path was almost 18 miles in length and up to 150 yards in width.  The tornado caused considerable tree damage in Union City.  Trees were uprooted and multiple trees fell on homes causing additional damage.  Some of the uprooted trees damaged road surfaces.  The strong winds from the tornado also caused damage to roofs and siding.   A building along Main Street lost it's brick facade.   A couple of homes west of Union City lost large sections of roofing.  A couple of farm buildings were also damaged.  Damage elsewhere along the damage path consisted of mainly downed trees.  Peak winds were estimated around 105 mph making this an EF1 tornado.  Two minor injuries were reported.

Some trees were toppled along the damage path and two homes and a garage in Custar sustained roof damage.  Damaging straight line winds accompanied the tornado and downed trees elsewhere in Custar.  The tornado had a damage path nearly a mile in length and up to 50 yards in width.  This tornado was rated an EF0.

A residential property on route 193 and Tower Road was inundated by about 6 inches into the first floor of the property destroying most of their belongings. An office building nearby was also under water.  The flooding was the result of a small slow moving thunderstorm that had rainfall rates measured by a nearby COOP observer at 4.8 per hour.

As a result of heavy rains overnight ��� up to 3 inches in some areas ��� several roads were closed Tuesday July 9th due to high water. The Richland County Sheriff said that 5th Street in downtown Mansfield had flooded, and the fire department evacuated people from homes using boats. There was also flooding on Park Avenue East where roads and railroad tracks were underwater. Some cars were nearly submerged. The Clear Fork River in Shelby forced the fire department out of their station and put about a foot of water over the main road through town. Residents in Bellville were also flooded, according to the sheriff.

In Morrow County, The Whetstone Creek flooded its banks in Mt. Gilead. The Lee Street apartments in Mt. Gilead were flooded. Seventy-five people in 20 units were affected by the flood waters. Flooding problems were reported along State Routes 95 and 314 in Morrow County, high water on another part of State Route 95 at the Knox-Morrow County line and the Richland-Morrow County line. A farm north of Mt. Gilead had over a dozen horses forced to swim to dry land as the property was inundated.

In Knox County water had closed sections of Waterford, Quaker, Darlington, Yankee, Toms, Lock, Orange Hill, Lanning, Wally and Knox Lake roads. According to the Knox County EMA, Fredericktown and Danville were hit the hardest in that area. Campers were moved to higher ground at Camp Kokosing after the North Branch of the Kokosing River inundated the campground with 3 to 5 feet of water. Several camper trailers were inundated.

Several roads in Morrow County were closed due to high water. A swath of 2 to upwards of 3.5 inches of rain fell over portions of central Morrow County the night of the 8th. The rain fell over already saturated soil and the rivers and creeks were running high prior to the onset of new rain. By daybreak in Mt. Gilead 75 people were evacuated from apartments and 3 from trailers as flood waters inundated their property. In total 20 properties saw water inundate the first floor with a few inches of water. The fairgrounds flooded.
A waterspout was observed on Lake Erie just to the northwest of Vermilion.

Widespread flood was occurring across the county with the worst conditions in Crestline after an estimated four inches of rain fell in 4 hours.  Six homes and one business along Front Street had flood waters into the first floor. Several Streets were closed.

After 3 to 4 inches of rain fell over the Black Fork of the Mohican River on the evening of the 8th, it pushed the river out of its banks in the town of Shelby. The town was cut off from east to west. Main Street was closed and the Fire Department and several businesses were evacuated. Numerous homes sustained water damage.

Widespread flooding was reported in eastern Crawford County. In Galion, the water inundated Heise Park as the Olentangy River tributaries were overwhelmed. Ohio 309 from North East Street at Chalres Street to Harding Way East was inundated and closed.  A house on Olentangy Court was inundated in the first floor. In Bucyrus, it was the Sandusky River that came out of its banks flooding several basements. A vehicle was damaged as the driver entered flooded Knauss Road. North Sandusky Ave, River Street, Temple Road, and Bethel Roads were closed. All of this flooding was the result of 2 to 4 inches of rainfall from the evening of the 8th.

According to the Knox County EMA, Fredericktown and Danville were hit the hardest in that area after an estimated 2 to 4 inches of rain fell on the evening of the 8th. A campground on the Kokosing River was inundated.  Knox County flooded roads include S.R. 205, S.R. 95 north of Tom's Road, and Knox Lake Road.

Two and a half inches of rain fell over saturated ground in Mansfield Ohio on the evening of the 8th and into the early morning hours of the 9th. Most of the flooding that occurred in Mansfield was caused by the excessive runoff and poor drainage. The fire department evacuated homes using boats along 5th Street in downtown. |Flooding on Park Avenue East put roads and railroad tracks underwater. Some cars were submerged. On Mulberry Street, a few inches of water inundated the first floor of some businesses.  The rain caused the already swollen Rocky Fork, a tributary to the Mohican River, to come out of its banks in the northern part of town.

An EF1 tornado touched just northwest of the Ursuline College campus around 3:35 am.  The tornado continued south southeast across a part of the campus, crossed Fairmount Boulevard and finally lifted as it moved across a country club.  Substantial damage was done to a gymnasium on the campus.  The tornado caused a wall to collapse and tore off a part of the roof.  Other buildings nearby sustained lesser amounts of roof damage.  Many trees were also toppled or snapped along the damage path which was up to 200 yards in width and around a mile and a third in length.  There was also evidence of straight line wind damage in the area.
Thunderstorm winds downed two trees.  A farm wagon was also blown over.

High water was reported in Tully Township and Martel as heavy rainfall estimated between two and three inches fell over the areas on the night of the 9th and early morning hours of the 10th. Numerous washouts occurred due to excessive runoff and flowing water from tributaries of the Olentangy River. Access into Tully was cut off for the better part of the next day. The flooding occurred in areas that do not usually flood.

A tributary to the Clear Fork of the Mohican River rose rapidly during the overnight hours of the 9th to the 10th of July in Ontario Ohio. An estimated 2.5 fell in during the evening hours of the 9th, falling over saturated ground. The three day rainfall leading up to this event was close to 8, so conditions were ripe for maximum runoff. A resident along Rock Road awoke in the early morning hours to water filling her home. They were trapped in the home with 6 feet of water in the first floor before the water receded almost as quickly as it rose. The residents lost their belongings and sustained significant damage to their home, but there were fortunately no injuries.

A weak EF0 tornado touched down west of Rowsburg near the intersection of County Roads 1302 and 251.  The tornado continued east southeast for about a mile before dissipating on the north end of Rowsburg.  The damage path indicates that the tornado was probably intermittent and at tree top level.  A barn was toppled near the beginning of the damage path and a house in Rowsburg was also heavily damaged by fallen trees.  The barn appears to have been toppled from a combination of tornadic and straight line winds.  Five livestock animals were killed in the barn collapse with several more injured.  Many trees were downed along the damage path and large swaths of corn were flattened.  The damage path from the tornado was no more than 15 yards wide but damage from the accompanying straight line downburst winds was more than a half mile in width at times.  The damage path was a little over a mile in length.

A line of thunderstorms producing winds in excess of 70 mph raced east across Seneca County causing significant damage.  Thousands of trees and limbs were downed across the county and large swaths of corn were flattened in fields.  Nearly every community in the county sustained damage and hundreds of homes and buildings were damaged.  Over two dozen farm buildings were leveled in the county.  The Bellevue area was especially hard hit with damage reported on nearly every street.  At least a half dozen homes in the city were heavily damaged by fallen trees and dozens of others sustained lesser damage, mainly from lost roofing or siding.  Businesses on Main Street had windows blown out and nearly the entire town lost power for an extended period.  It took almost five days for power to be fully restored.  Houses were also heavily damaged by fallen trees in Fremont and Clyde.  Many vehicles were damaged as well.  Scattered damage was also observed in the rural portions of the county.  Power outages affecting traffic signals and roads closed by downed trees severely hampered travel in the county after this storm.  At least four people had to rescued after they became stranded in their vehicles by downed power lines.  U.S Route 20 was closed in several locations.  Clean up costs from this storm were substantial.  Ten townships, four villages and two cities applied for nearly $1 million in disaster relief.
A funnel cloud was observed.

The damage was especially heavy in the northeast corner of the county from Reedtown north to Flat Rock.  A lot of downed trees were also reported in the Attica area. The tornado continued east northeast for just over three quarters of a mile and lifted near the intersection of Gardner and Kilbourne Streets.  The tornado may have been at tree top level because most of the damage was confined to trees and rooftops.  Many homes sustained minor damage, mainly from lost roofing and siding. The towns of Milan, Oxford, and Groton townships were the most impacated by the heavy rains of July 10th. Doppler radar estimates between 3 and 4 inches of rain fell within an hour and a half with strong storms that moved through Erie County. Flooding was so widespread that local and county officials were advising the public to stay off the roads. The major thru ways of Ohio 113, Ohio 99, and U.S. 250 were closed. Drivers trying to circumvent the area were left with few options, as most of the surrounding roads had varying degrees of flooding. Portions of Patten Tract, Mason, Strecker, Ransom, Thomas and Kelley roads were overrun with pools of  inches-deep water. A few homes were inundated in the first floor by flood waters, but the majority of the home flood damage was the result of basement flooding.

Torrential rain with fell on July 10th over mainly southern portions of Sandusky County with radar estimates around 3 inches fell in 1.5 hours. Widespread rapidly developing flooding occurred. Bellevue Police reported most of the town was flooded with several cars stuck in the water. State RT 105, U.S. 6 between U.S. 23 and State Rt. 53, Route 53 near the Ohio Turnpike, and State Rt. 19 near County Road 213 were closed from the flooding.

Intense rainfall of rates estimated around 4 inches per hour over downtown Cleveland caused a section of wall to collapse at Tower City. The collapsed wall forced the Red Line trains to stop operations for a short while.

Intense rainfall rates over east Cleveland caused a washout of the major thru-way Martin Luther King Blvd in the University Circle region. A significant portion of the southbound portion of the pavement was washed out.

Nearly 4.5 inches of rain was reported over southern Cuyahoga County. The resulting flooding was primarily to roads and infrastructure, but there was some basement flooding mainly in the Berea area. Some impacts include widespread metropark flooding. The Canal Road in Valley View was closed from Rockside to Stone due to sinkhole conditions. In Macedonia there was a partial bridge collapse.

The Norwalk Creek exceeded its banks as it was overwhelmed by runoff from torrential rain. The creek rose quickly and thretened a few homes and businesses which were inundated to their first level. A woman was rescued from her vehicle as the flowing creek overran Lover's Lane Road.

On Wednesday afternoon, July 10, the City of Akron experienced 3 to 4 inches of rain in an hour and a half.  Flooding occurred causing the closings of roadways and expressways.  Along with the roadway flooding, the City received reports of nearly 200 flooded basements.  Widespread flooding was reported throughout the city and numerous homes, businesses, and vehicles were inundated by the rain.

Heavy rainfall over and upstream of the Copley Township community in Summit County produced significant flooding. Torrential rainfall of an estimated 4 inches per hour fell over the area in the afternoon hours of the 10th. This was the 17th consecutive day of rain, so runoff was high as the grounds were saturated. In all, the township has a list of 37 residents who experienced damage and loss from the flooding, most notably on the Sunnyacres Road area where a flooded storm water ditch overflowed.

High water closed most roads in Shalersville after an estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain fell within one hour. This rainfall was after 16 consecutive days with rain in the region. Subsequently the saturated ground could not absorb the water and widespread flooding resulted. The water came up so quickly that emergency officials had to evacuate homeowners. Several people became stranded in their cars or homes. Hardest hit areas include Wentworth Street in the Bolingbrook neighborhood and Aurora East where water was several feet deep in homes. The flood waters inundated about half of the 350 homes. The waters receded within an hour or two.

Flooding was significant across the Streetsboro community on the evening of July 10th. Some of the roads that were flooded included Route 303, Russell Drive, Luke Drive, portions of Camelot Village and Fronek Road. Over a dozen cars were caught in the flood waters, and one family had to be rescued after being swept off the road and into a creek. The intensity of the rain caused several building alarms set off by high water and some traffic signals out. A nearby rain gauge measured 3.25 inches from the storm, however this rain fell quickly onto saturated ground cover. Updated storm drainage systems supported most of the runoff which reduced impacts to homes and businesses.

Heavy rainfall produced widespread flooding in Ravenna with the hardest hit area along Dawley Road in the township. Other areas include South Chestnut Street, Spruce Road and Hazen Avenue in the city. The rainfall estimates are between 3 and 4 inches of rainfall which fell on the 10th.

Heavy rainfall estimated around 3 inches fell over southern Trumbull County. This resulted in widespread flooding as the ground had been wet from recent rain. The Eagle Creek in Braceville came out of banks and flooded most low lying roads and a few homes on Barcley Messerly Road. A few water rescues  were needed for motorists in Braceville and Newton Falls. Crossroads in Newton Falls at Warren Ravenna Road, Taft Avenue and Wilson Avenue, had water standing as high as the mailbox of one residence. Dozens of basements were inundated in the two towns.

Residents along the west branch of the Rocky River were inundated by flood waters on the afternoon and early evening hours of July 10th. Champion Creek overflowed, causing closures at West Smith and River Styx roads and inundated a few homes. The Chippewa Lake area was flooded as the sewer backed up from excessive runoff. In Montville Township, the Medina Fire Department rescued two residents from homes along River Styx Road.

Widespread flooding occurred across the city of Medina on the evening of the 10th. In addition to a dozen homes being inundated, the city���s municipal court basement was flooded. Residential basement flooding was worst on Forest Meadows Drive, South Court and Huntington streets. Medina police received reports of vehicles stalled along West Smith Road between South Elmwood Avenue and South Court Street because an irrigation ditch collecting water next to the railroad tracks overflowed.

Heavy rains that moved over Lorain County most notably impacted the La Grange area in the southeast portion of the county. In this area radar estimates around 2 inches of rain fell within 45 minutes. Floating cars were reported on Whitehead and Whitney roads, causing the intersection to close. At least one home was significantly inundated, while a half dozen other homes had flooding in their basements.

During the peak of the flooding a large portion of Wooster and Apple Creek were underwater. This included portions of the Wayne County Fairgrounds and Schellin Park. The high water forced the closure of numerous roads across the area including Freedlander, Grosjean, Timken, Baurer Roads and Prairie Lane, Spruce Street, South Bever Street, and Old Lincoln Way. Residents on North Baurer Road and Spruce Street were forced to evacuate. Businesses along Freedlander Road were also evacuated. Four of the city's waste water treatment facilities life stations went down from flood waters. One of the wastewater treatment plants had 6 to 8 feet of sewage in the buidling. In Apple Creek, the creek came out of banks and shut down some local roads. A home and a vehicle where inundated in that town.

Flash flooding was reported along Route 91 near Summit County fairgrounds. At least 2 cars swept off road into ditches. Water was up to roof of cars. The city received about 10 reports of basement floodings.

Law Enforcement reported numerous road closures due to torrential rain from storms that moved through the area between 330 PM and 430 PM. NWS radar estimates rainfall amounts of 3 to 4 inches fell over the area during that time. A steel bridge along Keepville Road was completely under water and Route 18 was closed. Albion Local Officials requested evacuations near the Albion Boro Park. In Cranesville, just north of Albion, the sewer system was compromised.

After seventeen consecutive days with rain, the heavy rain that moved through northeastern Marion County on July 10th 2013 was enough to produce one more round of flooding. In a matter of 15 minutes, residents say it went from standing water to a flash flood with more than a foot of rushing water from the Hell Branch Run into portions of Caledonia. Some businesses and basements were inundated with water and mud.

Over two weeks of consecutive rain was peaked by torrential rain on the 9th and 10th of July where brought widespread flooding to Richland County. The most impacted towns were Shelby, Mansfield, Ontario, Lexington, Bellville and Butler ���with reported damage to homes and businesses. There was some road damage due to fast moving water. Major flooding at the Pleasant Hill Marina and lake caused evacuation of all campers and boats in that area. Radar estimates put the average rainfall in the county around 4 inches in 48 hours, with locally higher amounts of 6 to 8 inches. The heaviest rain fell over the Black and Clear Forks of the Mohican River, which resulted in widespread flooding for communities along those bodies of water. The period of flooding occurred during peak tourist season and resulted in a notably monetary loss as the river and surrounding campsites were closed for recreational sports.
A line of storms with heavy rain moved through Crawford County on the 10th of July. Six homes with first floor flooding in the Village of Crestline.

Seventeen days of consecutive rain brought widespread flooding to Crawford County. The hardest  hit towns were Bucyrus and Crestline. In Bucyrus, the Sandusky River came out of its banks resulting flooding of the Harmon Park soccer complex, and surrounding homes on Clinton and Lane Streets. North Sandusky Ave and Water Street were closed. Elsewhere in the county numerous roads were closed and part of Ohio 19 and Brokensword were closed. Most of the county had received between 3.5 and 7 inches of rain over a 48 hour period, with the heaviest rain falling over Crestline. In Galion numerous roads were closed.

During the early morning hours of the 20th, specifically between 230 am and 530 am, torrential rain fell over extreme northeast Cuyahoga County and most of Lake County. The showers were enhanced by the warm and moist air over Lake Erie, and subsequently produced rainfall rates that exceeded the storm drainage systems in any populated communities affected.  Rainfall reports ranged from 3.44 in Madison to 6 inches in Fairport Harbor. In Kirtland, an observer measured 2.20 inches between 3 am and 5 am. The rain came after two previous weeks of wet weather which had raised the water table and saturated the ground. The rainfall produced flooding in over 500 basements with the majority being sanitary sewer backups. One basement's wall caved in causing structural damage to the house. Overall 13 properties in Mentor were classified as having suffered major structural damage. The most damage was reported in western Lake between Mentor and Wickliffe.  In Kirtland Hills the Baldwin Road sustained structural damage from washout. In Concord 50 homes were flooded and were not due to sewer backups.  In Cuyahoga County, Euclid was one of the highly affected areas, with more than 5 inches of rain falling in a short amount of time. That left some residents with anywhere from several inches to several feet of water in their homes. The wastewater treatment plant was under 20 feet of water and much of the equipment needed to be replaced. In all over 3,500 properties sustained some form of flood inundation.

A weak EF1 tornado touched down in rural Reed Township near the intersection of County Road 27 and Township Road 122.  The tornado continued intermittently on the ground for about six miles before crossing into Huron County.  Damage along the damage path consisted mainly of downed trees, although some structures did sustain significant damage.   Several barns lost sections of roofing.  One home near the initial touchdown had a second story wall partially collapse.  The attached garage on one home lost its garage door and was lifted from its foundation.  There was also evidence of extensive straight wind damage along the path.  Crop damage, especially to corn, was significant.

A weak EF1 tornado crossed into Huron County from Seneca County near the intersection of State Route 269 and Section Line Road.  The tornado then continued intermittently on the ground for about four miles before lifting near the Bellevue Reservoir.  Damage along the path in Huron County consisted of mainly downed trees.  There was also evidence of extensive straight line wind damage along the path.  Crop damage, especially to corn, was significant.

An EF0 tornado touched down southeast of Kansas just to the east of the intersection of State Route 636 and Township Road 36.  The tornado was only briefly on the ground but tore the roof off of a mobile and damaged a nearby barn.  A camper on property was also overturned.  Many trees were also toppled and some corn was blown down in a field.  The damage path was no more than 100 yards in length.  A trained spotted witnessed the touchdown.

Torrential rainfall on July 10th ended the streek of 13 days of measurable rain in the Barberton-Norton region, and ending it with the highest rainfall amounts measuring during that time. Almost seven inches of rain fell in the two weeks prior, and on the 10th rainfall amounts in the basin measured between 2 to 3 inches which fell in the hour between 230 and 330 PM. This extreme rainfall rate fell over already saturated ground and swollen stream and creeks, resulting in rapid runoff and flooding. Heavy rainfall of this magnitude overwhelmed the existing stormwater systems with extensive street flooding throughout Barberton.  In many areas of Barberton the flooded streets drained within a few hours leaving many flooded basements, garages and yards.  After the flash flooding had stopped, the upstream routed water caused the flood waters to continue a slow rise in Barberton. These areas began flooding during the night of July 10 and by the morning of July 11th flooding was reaching into new areas.  Flood waters in most areas receded by Sunday July 14th leaving behind large areas of the City needing clean-up operations. Unseasonably cold air moving across warm Lake Erie caused lake effect snow showers to develop during the evening of October 23rd. The snow briefly tapered off during the middle portion of the 24th and then picked up again during the afternoon. The snow finally ended for good during the early morning hours of 25th. The trees across the region still had leaves and the snow caused considerable damage. Hundreds of trees and limbs were downed resulting in many power outages. Accumulations of 4 to 8 inches were reported from eastern Cuyahoga County. During the peak of the event, thunder and lightning were reported and snow rates approached two inches per hour. Several airplanes on final approach to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport flew through the snow bands and were struck by lightning. No injuries were reported and all of the planes were able to safely land.  For much of the area, this was the first time during the Fall that temperatures had fallen to freezing. Nearly 50,000 electric customers lost power during this event. In Cuyahoga County, most of the outages were in Lyndhurst, Cleveland Heights and Mayfield Heights. It took till October 26th for the power to be fully restored. Many accidents resulted from this early season snow and travel was a problem in some areas.

Warm rain of around an inch to an inch and a half melted all the snowpack during the 24 hours preceding the flash floods. The earlier rain saturated the ground and filled the storm drainage systems in the city of Tiffin. As a round of moderate rainfall moved in on the evening of the 22nd, it produced overflow and flooding in the city. The viaduct on North Washington Street was flooded and closed, and Main Street near Heidelberg University's senior apartments was flooded. Areas throughout Seneca County experiencing high water were CR 594; SR 587, north of TR 96; SR 231, south of CR 6; SR 4, north and south of Attica; North SR 53 at CR 32; SR 101 at CR 179; SR 19 at CR 32; and Euclid Avenue. Also, US 224, east of SR 100, was closed.

The Sandusky River at Tiffin came out of its banks after a heavy rain event on the 21st and 22nd. The river 11.11 feet, 0.61 feet above moderate flood stage. Flooding impacted Route 53 north of U.S. 224. Floodwaters also inundated Township Road 131. In the city of Tiffin, Water Street, Marlyn Street, Front Street, and Davis Street were inundated. There was one fatality on Maryln Street due to the flooding.

The Blanchard River at Findlay Ohio crested at 15.58 feet on Sunday the 22nd of December according to a USGS post storm survey. This crest is the 8th highest on record and two feet above major flood stage. The level, though significant, did not reach the level needed for massive evacuations which is 16 feet.Significant parts of Findlay were underwater and numerous state highways were closed. The Eagle Creek, a tributary to joins with the Blanchard River in Findlay, also reached major flood stage at 11.4 feet. The highways that were closed included U.S. 68 on the south side. Four homes sustained major damage, 2 minor based on FEMA's damage assessment criteria. Other homes were flooded in their basements. In all, 45 homes experienced flood damage.

Road crews shut down major intersections in and around Findlay during the evening of December 21st. The off/on ramp of State Route 15 was flooded. Portions of Tiffin Avenue and Route 224 were shut down blocking most traffic into the city. Interstate 75 flooded and closed by flash flooding just north of Findlay.

Several roads throughout the county were closed because of high water along Ohio 100 southeast of Bucyrus and near the village of Monnett in the southern part of the county. Ohio 19 north of Bucyrus was closed.

Red Cross reports downtown Carey Ohio was flooded by heavy rain on the night of December 21st into 22nd. One home was flooded as a result of 1.5-2 of rain falling within a 6 hour time frame that evening before. The main street in Carey, U.S. 23, was closed by the flooding.

Heavy rain around 2 inches in 6 hours caused the Whetstone Creek to flash flood during the early morning hours of the 22nd. The Whetstone Creek runs from the Mt. Gilead Lakes and Mt. Gilead Upper Lake Dam through southern Mt. Gilead. A dog shelter just west of Main Street was flooded with 18 of water from the flood. The dogs had been removed before the flood waters crested. The Morrow County Fairgrounds inundated as well.

The Scioto River at La Rue in Marion County Ohio experienced it's worst flood in 50 years (03/05/63 15.95 feet) when it crested at a stage of 14.18 feet on December 22nd. This major flood surpassed the more recent floods February 28, 2011 by only 0.09 feet. The Scioto River will flood the outskirts of town before reaching the city limits. When the river comes out of banks, it quickly fills up the low lying town. The Kiwanis Village retirement community, an apartment complex for seniors inundated as much as 2 feet in some units, and reached the roofs of cars left in the parking lot.  100 people had to be evacuated. Access in and out of town were cut off by flood waters. The floods were the result of heavy rain tha fell on December 21st over saturated ground. Any snow had long since melted and the ground was not frozen. The basin average rainfall was around 3 inches.

An EF0 tornado touched down near Lime City Road just to the north of U.S. Route 20 in Perrysburg.  The tornado continued east northeast reaching EF2 intensity as it neared the intersection of State Route 795 and Oregon Road.  Two warehouse buildings had walls blown down and lost large sections of roofing.  A gas station at the intersection of State Route 795 and Oregon Road was heavily damaged.  Several vehicles at the gas station were damaged.  Other businesses in the immediate vicinity also sustained roof damage.  After causing extensive damage to a couple homes in a residential neighborhood just north of State Route 795, the tornado weakened to EF0 intensity.  It then remained on the ground as either an EF0 or EF1 tornado for another four and half miles before moving into Lucas County near Northwood.  It damaged several more homes and some apartment buildings before entering Lucas County.  Most of this damage was from lost roofing and siding.  Dozens of trees were downed along the damage path which was just over seven miles long and up to a 100 yards in width in Wood County.  Many vehicles including a couple of recreational vehicles were damaged by the strong winds or flying debris.

A EF0 tornado crossed into Lucas County from Wood County just to the west of Interstate 280 in Northwood.  The tornado continued to the northeast and intensified to EF1 intensity as it moved across the Pearson Metropark.  It tore the roof off of a house and damaged another home in this area.  The tornado briefly intensified to EF2 as it neared Seaman Street in Oregon.  The tornado made a left turn at that time and finally lifted as it crossed Corduroy Road north of Oregon.  The tornado damaged many homes in Oregon.  Most of the damage was from lost roofing or siding but at least two homes were damaged enough to be considered destroyed.   The tornado was on the ground for over four miles in Lucas County.  The damage path was up to a 100 yards in width.  Dozens of trees were downed along the damage path and many vehicles were damaged by the strong winds or flying debris.

An EF0 tornado touched down east of Elmore along West Yeasting Road just to the west of State Route 590.  The tornado moved northeast and briefly intensified to EF1 intensity as it crossed State Route 590.  A barn near this location was leveled.  The tornado continued on the ground for another half mile or so and then lifted.  The damage path was around three quarters of a mile in length and no more than 75 yards in width.  Damage consisted mainly of a few downed trees and limbs.

An EF1 tornado touched down northwest of North Baltimore along Quarry Road to the west of Liberty Hi Road.  A home near the initial touchdown was partially destroyed when a portion of its roof tore off allowing a wall to collapse.  The tornado continued on the ground for around a mile before lifting.  Damage elsewhere along the damage path consisted of a few downed trees.  The parent thunderstorm responsible for this tornado later produced another tornado near Jerry City.

An EF1 tornado touched down east of Jerry City near the intersection of Main Street and Huffman Road.  The tornado then continued east for around one and a third miles and lifted after crossing Cloverdale Road.  A mobile home along Main Street was destroyed and a couple of other homes and buildings in the area lost roofing and siding.  Damage along the remainder of the damage path consisted of mainly downed trees.  The parent thunderstorm responsible for this tornado earlier produced a tornado near North Baltimore.

Lake effect snow showers began before dawn on December 31st. Periods of moderate to heavy snow occurred throughout the day. The snow continued into the New Year with heavy accumulations on January 1st and 2nd as an area of low pressure passed to the south of the area. Inland areas of Erie County saw 6 or more inches of snow by midnight on the 1st. Westerly winds gusted to as much as 30 mph during the day. This caused near whiteout conditions at times along with considerable blowing and drifting.

Police in Rocky River reported an ice jam on the Rocky River near the Metropark marina. The ice jam broke free around 1 pm and travelled about 2 miles to the mouth of the river into Lake Erie. The lake had been frozen over, but strong southwest gales were able to break up the mouth of the Rocky River sufficiently to allow the ice jam to move out of the river. Numerous docks and boats were damaged along the river, including a marina in the Metropark.

An area of low pressure moved east across the Tennessee Valley on January 2nd. A trough extending north from this low caused snow to develop just before midnight on January 2nd. The trough moved into western Pennsylvania during the late afternoon hours of the 2nd causing the flow to become northerly off of Lake Erie. Snowfall intensities began to increase during the morning hours with visibilities dropping below a quarter mile for several hours during the afternoon and early evening hours. Snowfall rates during this time approached two inches per hour. The evening commute in the Cleveland area was very difficult and dozens of accidents were reported. The snow finally tapered off from west to east during the late evening hours. Northeast to north winds gusted to as much as 25 mph during this event causing a lot of blowing and drifting. Six to eight inches of snow fell from Lorain County east across the Cleveland Metropolitan area and Lake and Geauga Counties and into Ashtabula Counties. Much of this accumulation fell between 1 and 6 pm. A peak total of 7.8 inches was reported near Lorain.

An area of low pressure moved east across the Tennessee Valley on January 1st and 2nd.  A warm front from the low lifted into western Ohio causing snow to develop early on the 1st.  The snow continued all day on the 1st and much of the 2nd before finally tapering off during the evening hours.  Periods of moderate to heavy snow occurred during the evening hours of the 1st and morning hours of the 2nd.  Heavy snow fell on most of the Toledo Metropolitan area.  Accumulations dropped off quickly to the south and east.  A total of 9.4 inches of snow was measured at Toledo Express Airport with 6.8 inches of that total falling by midnight on the 2nd.  North to northeast winds gusted to as much as 30 mph during this event and caused considerable blowing and drifting.  Holiday travel was hampered by this storm as many accidents were reported.

Snow developed over northwestern Ohio around daybreak on the 5th. Periods of moderate to heavy snow were then reported throughout the day. Snowfall rates exceeded an inch per hour at times. The snow briefly ended during the early morning hours of the 6th but resumed again after daybreak. The snow ended for good around midday on the 6th. Northwest winds gusted to as much as 30 mph on the 5th with westerly winds in excess of 40 mph on the 6th. Near blizzard conditions were reported for many hours and travel was nearly impossible at times.  The heaviest snow fell across western Lucas County. At Toledo Express Airport a total of 13.0 inches fell on the 5th and 6th with 9.4 inches on 5th. 9.3 inches of snow fell at Sylvania. Temperatures plummeted on the 6th with temperatures falling below zero by mid morning. The combination of frigid temperatures and strong winds made clean up of the snow nearly impossible. Schools in Northwest Ohio were closed on both the 6th and 7th.

An area of strong low pressure moved east across the Great Lakes on January 25th. A cold front trailing this low swept east across northern Ohio during the morning hours. Snow developed ahead of this front during the early morning and then intensified around daybreak as the front moved through. Southwest winds gusted to as much as 35 mph ahead of the front. Northwest winds developed behind the frontal passage and by midday the snow had transitioned to lake effect snow showers. The snow showers intensified just before the evening commute causing near blizzard conditions at times. Visibilities were less than a quarter mile for most of the late afternoon and early evening hours. Snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour crippled the Cleveland Metropolitan area and made for a rough evening commute. The snow lessened around 7 pm and tapered to flurries shortly after that. Snowfall totals across Cuyahoga, Geauga and northern Summit and Medina Counties ranged from 6 to locally 9 inches. Much of that fell during the afternoon. In Cuyahoga County totals included 10.0 inches at Broadview Heights; 9.0 inches at Solon; 7.5 inches in Garfield Heights; 7.0 inches in Lakewood and 6.8 inches in Parma. In addition, the gusty winds caused considerable blowing and drifting. Dozens of accidents were reported across the area and commute times were two to three times normal.

A dangerously cold air mass settled over northern Ohio from January 27-28th with wind chill values of -25 to -30 degrees during the early morning hours of January 28th.  The wind chill at Toledo dropped to -29 degrees between 2 and 3 am on January 28th with west to southwest winds of 5 to 15 mph.  A record low temperature of -10 degrees was set that morning and tied the previous record for that day from 1977.  Conditions started to improve by late morning as temperatures gradually recovered into the single digits but dropped below zero again overnight.  All area school were closed on January 28th with most school also closed on January 29th.

A record low temperature of -10 degrees was set that morning and tied the previous record for that day from 1977. Conditions started to improve by late morning as temperatures gradually recovered into the single digits but dropped below zero again overnight. All area school were closed on January 28th with most school also closed on January 29th.

A fast moving area of low pressure raced east across the lower Great Lakes during the evening hours of February 17th and the morning hours of the 18th. Snow associated with this low began over Northeast Ohio during the evening of the 17th. The snow quickly intensified and then continued through the early morning hours of the 18th. The snow was heavy at times with visibilities less than a quarter mile and accumulations of an inch or more per hour.  The snow quickly tapered off from west to east beginning around daybreak on the 18th and by mid morning had ended across the entire area. Southwest winds gusted to as much as 35 mph during the first half of the event. Winds became westerly and slowly diminished as the the surface low passed just to the north. Considerable blowing and drifting was reported causing difficult road conditions. The morning commute was very slow and most of the schools in Northeast Ohio closed on the 18th. Snowfall totals from Lorain County eastward across the Cleveland and Akron Metropolitan areas to Trumbull County ranged from 6 to 8 inches. A peak total in the county for this storm was 7.5 inches at Lakewood.
